construction: Divide width and height into three equal parts. Lines land at 33.3% and 66.7% of each dimension, whatever the frame ratio
what_it_claims: That placing the subject on a thirds line or intersection makes a picture more pleasing
what_the_evidence_says: Named by John Thomas Smith in 1797, not invented by him. Amirshahi et al. 2014 computed thirds scores across 1082 photographs, 727 paintings and 606 near-random scenes: aesthetic ratings correlated only weakly with subjective thirds scores and not at all with computed ones. Hoh & Zhang 2023 ran forced-choice between centred and thirds-placed subjects and participants overwhelmingly preferred centred. Eye-tracking work finds trained photographers rate thirds-compliant images as more interesting while novices are insensitive. Read together: a producer-side convention that reads as competently shot to a trained eye, not a driver of lay preference
use_when: A lifestyle still that needs a copy band; when you want the asset to read as conventionally well shot
do_not_use_when: An ecommerce packshot, a wide frame, or any asset a platform will centre-crop

construction: phi = (1 + sqrt 5) / 2 = 1.6180339887. Its reciprocal is 0.6180339887. Lines land at 38.2% and 61.8% of each dimension
what_it_claims: That phi placement is mathematically and therefore aesthetically superior to thirds
what_the_evidence_says: The construction is correct arithmetic. The superiority claim has to survive the size of the difference it is asserting: 38.2% against 33.3% is 4.9 percentage points, which on a 1080 px width is 53 px — about a finger-width at phone viewing distance — and on 1920 px is 94 px. No study in the thirds literature resolves a 5%-of-frame perturbation, so no study supports preferring one over the other. Markowsky 1992 shows most claims about phi in art and architecture are false or seriously misleading; parts of the Parthenon fall outside the golden rectangle enthusiasts draw over it
use_when: As a sizing ratio: a type scale of 16 → 26 → 42 px, a margin-to-column ratio, a 61.8 / 38.2 image-to-copy split
do_not_use_when: As a placement rule you defend to a client on the grounds that the mathematics makes it better

construction: A logarithmic spiral inscribed in nested golden rectangles, dropped over a finished photograph
what_it_claims: That the subject falling on the spiral confirms the composition works
what_the_evidence_says: Unfalsifiable as used. A spiral can be scaled, rotated and mirrored into more than eight orientations, so something in almost any photograph will land on some arm of it. A test that cannot fail is not a test. The self-similarity that generates the spiral is real — removing the square from a golden rectangle leaves a golden rectangle — but that property says nothing about where a subject should sit
do_not_use_when: Any time it is used after the fact to justify a frame that was composed some other way

construction: Draw both full diagonals. From each corner draw a line perpendicular to the opposite full diagonal until it meets an edge; the rectangle it cuts off is the reciprocal, a scaled rotated copy of the whole. The four reciprocal diagonals crossing the two full diagonals give four primary intersections — Hambidge called them the eyes. For width W and height H the eye sits at x = W·H² / (W² + H²), y = H·W² / (W² + H²) from the corner
what_it_claims: That Greek vases and the Parthenon were composed on root rectangles, and that the grid inherits their authority
what_the_evidence_says: Split the claim. The historical half is contested on the same grounds as every phi-in-antiquity claim. The construction half is genuinely useful and needs no history: every line it produces is in whole-number relationship to the frame, so the grid is commensurate with the ratio instead of imposing 3×3 on it. The consequence is measurable — the wider the frame, the further from centre the eye sits: 50% at 1:1, 30.8% at 3:2, 24% at 16:9, 14.9% at scope. Thirds says 33.3% at every ratio, which is why widescreen composed on thirds looks wrong. The converse is the useful cross-check: set h squared = 2 w squared and the eye lands on exactly 1/3, so on ISO A-series paper the two grids coincide and the choice is empty
use_when: 16:9 and wider — key art, video, any frame where thirds visibly fails
do_not_use_when: A square or near-square frame, where the eye computes to the centre and the grid tells you nothing

construction: The frame centre, adjusted for the fact that a subject's visual mass is not its bounding box: align the mass, not the outline
what_it_claims: That centring is the safe default and reads as neutral rather than unconsidered
what_the_evidence_says: Supported where it matters commercially. Hoh & Zhang 2023 found a preference for centred subjects in forced choice, and central fixation bias is well documented. For an ecommerce packshot it is also the only placement that survives a blind platform crop, which is a mechanical argument rather than an aesthetic one
use_when: Packshots, marketplace tiles, range arrays, anything that will be centre-cropped by a platform you do not control
do_not_use_when: An editorial frame where the negative space is carrying the message

construction: The corner-to-corner diagonals of the frame, used as a path to lay the subject along rather than a point to place it on
what_it_claims: That a subject along the diagonal reads as dynamic and a subject on a horizontal reads as static
what_the_evidence_says: A craft convention with a mechanical basis: a diagonal is the longest straight path across a frame, so it holds a longer read. Related evidence that does hold: the eye prefers the smoothest continuous path, and direction changes along it should stay under 45 degrees — a change over about 90 degrees terminates the path
use_when: Editorial and fashion spreads, and any frame where the subject is long
do_not_use_when: A frame with two competing diagonals crossing at 60–90 degrees; that produces a fixation stall at the crossing

construction: On a 1080 x 1920 canvas, take the most restrictive margin per side across platforms: top 269 px (Meta 14%), bottom 672 px (Meta 35%), left 65 px (Meta 6%), right 120 px (TikTok). The surviving core is 895 x 979 px
what_it_claims: That this is where a vertical asset may put anything that must be read
what_the_evidence_says: Measured, not aesthetic — but the figures are third-party caches and the platforms disagree with each other. TikTok's bottom margin is quoted anywhere between 120 px and 370 px, and TikTok's own guidance reportedly varies it by video dimension, caption length and ad format. What survives the disagreement is the derived number: the core is 42.3% of the frame and its centre sits at 47.5% of width and 39.5% of height. Cross-checking TikTok and Shorts band centres gives 44.5% each, so all three converge in the 39–45% range
use_when: Every 9:16 asset. Compose to 40% of frame height, not 50%
do_not_use_when: As a fixed constant. Re-verify against the platform's own help page before a paid flight
